question: Is a benchmark-and-measurement contribution (clause-level point-in-time retrieval evaluation plus retrieval-time valid-time gating) sufficient on its own, given that the gap it fills is already named in the literature?
description: Prior work explicitly names clause-granularity versioning as an unaddressed gap and prescribes point-in-time recovery, so the benchmark fills a recognized gap rather than revealing one. It is unclear whether a resource-and-measurement contribution of this kind is sufficient without a novel mechanism, or whether reviewers would require the retrieval-time enforcement to outperform representation-level temporal handling by a clear margin to count as a contribution.
confidence_basis: Three precedents of accepted measurement/resource contributions in this neighbourhood, each carrying a diagnostic result, plus the closest legal framework's explicit statement that it reports no empirical comparison. The verdict depends on results not yet produced, so it is narrowed rather than settled.
rationale: The review identifies the gap and the diagnostic criteria but reports no empirical comparison, so the measurement is genuinely missing; however the absence of a novel mechanism may cap the perceived contribution.
resolution: Partially resolved with a condition rather than a yes/no. A benchmark-and-measurement contribution is an established form here - SituatedQA's context-dependent QA dataset, a regulatory retrieval benchmark motivated by an understudied comparison, and a legal benchmark encoding temporal validity - but each carried a diagnostic finding that changed conclusions (a roughly 15-point drop, a reversal where BM25 beats hybrid on multihop queries, domain-specific overconfidence). Because the clause-granularity gap is already named and its detection criterion prescribed, the measurement alone is not sufficient; it becomes sufficient only if it yields a non-obvious result: a material contamination rate for the strongest published system, a decay-versus-validity divergence on non-latest-authoritative queries, or evidence that version-level scoring reorders systems that established metrics rank differently. Plan E004 is designed to test exactly that last condition, so the question is now operationalized and its answer depends on measurement.
